verses.zh: 以利户又说：
verses.en: Elihu answered:

verses.zh: 你们智慧人要听我的话；有知识的人要留心听我说。
verses.en: “Listen to my words, you wise men;hear[NOTE:1] me, you learned men.[NOTE:2]
notes: This speech of Elihu focuses on defending God. It can be divided into these sections: Job is irreligious (2-9), God is just (10-15), God is impartial and omniscient (16-30), Job is foolish to rebel (31-37).
Heb “give ear to me.”

verses.zh: 因为耳朵试验话语，好像上膛尝食物。
verses.en: For the ear assesses[NOTE:1] wordsas the mouth[NOTE:2] tastes food.
notes: The Hebrew word means “the men who know,” and without a complement it means “to possess knowledge.”
Or “examines; tests; tries; discerns.”

verses.zh: 我们当选择何为是，彼此知道何为善。
verses.en: Let us evaluate[NOTE:1] for ourselves what is right;[NOTE:2] let us come to know among ourselves what is good.
notes: Or “palate”; the Hebrew term refers to the tongue or to the mouth in general.
Elihu means “choose after careful examination.”

verses.zh: 约伯曾说：我是公义，　神夺去我的理；
verses.en: For Job says, ‘I am innocent,[NOTE:1] but God turns away my right.
notes: The word is מִשְׁפָּט (mishpat) again, with the sense of what is right or just.

verses.zh: 我虽有理，还算为说谎言的；我虽无过，受的伤还不能医治。
verses.en: Concerning my right, should I lie?[NOTE:1] My wound[NOTE:2] is incurable,although I am without transgression.’[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “righteous,” but in this context it means to be innocent or in the right.

The verb is the Piel imperfect of כָּזַב (kazav), meaning “to lie.” It could be a question: “Should I lie [against my right?]—when I am innocent.” If it is repointed to the Pual, then it can be “I am made to lie,” or “I am deceived.” Taking it as a question makes good sense here, and so emendations are unnecessary.

The Hebrew text has only “my arrow.” Some commentators emend that word slightly to get “my wound.” But the idea could be derived from “arrows” as well, the wounds caused by the arrows. The arrows are symbolic of God’s affliction.

verses.zh: 谁像约伯，喝讥诮如同喝水呢？
verses.en: Who is there like Job,who[NOTE:1] drinks derision[NOTE:2] like water?
notes: Heb “without transgression,” but this is parallel to the first part where the claim is innocence.
Heb “he drinks,” but coming after the question this clause may be subordinated.

verses.zh: 他与作孽的结伴，和恶人同行。
verses.en: He goes about[NOTE:1] in company[NOTE:2] with evildoers;he goes along[NOTE:3] with wicked men.[NOTE:4]
notes: The scorn or derision mentioned here is not against Job, but against God. Job scorns God so much, he must love it. So to reflect this idea, Gordis has translated it “blasphemy” (cf. NAB).
The perfect verb with the vav (ו) consecutive carries the sequence forward from the last description.
The word חֶבְרַה (khevrah, “company”) is a hapax legomenon. But its meaning is clear enough from the connections to related words and this context as well.
The infinitive construct with the ל (lamed) preposition may continue the clause with the finite verb (see GKC 351 §114.p).

verses.zh: 他说：人以　神为乐，总是无益。
verses.en: For he says, ‘It does not profit a manwhen he makes his delight with God.’[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “men of wickedness”; the genitive is attributive (= “wicked men”).

verses.zh: 所以，你们明理的人要听我的话。　神断不致行恶；全能者断不致作孽。
verses.en: “Therefore, listen to me, you men of understanding.[NOTE:1] Far be it from[NOTE:2] God to do wickedness,from the Almighty to do evil.
notes: Gordis, however, takes this expression in the sense of “being in favor with God.”
Heb “men of heart.” The “heart” is used for the capacity to understand and make the proper choice. It is often translated “mind.”

verses.zh: 他必按人所做的报应人，使各人照所行的得报。
verses.en: For he repays a person for his work,[NOTE:1] and according to the conduct of a person,he causes the consequences to find him.[NOTE:2]
notes: For this construction, see Job 27:5.
Heb “for the work of man, he [= God] repays him.”

verses.zh: 神必不作恶；全能者也不偏离公平。
verses.en: Indeed, in truth, God does not act wickedly,and the Almighty does not pervert justice.

verses.zh: 谁派他治理地，安定全世界呢？
verses.en: Who entrusted[NOTE:1] to him the earth?And who put him over[NOTE:2] the whole world?
notes: Heb “he causes it to find him.” The text means that God will cause a man to find (or receive) the consequences of his actions.

The verb פָּקַד (paqad) means “to visit; to appoint; to number.” Here it means “to entrust” for care and governing. The implication would be that there would be someone higher than God—which is what Elihu is repudiating by the rhetorical question. No one entrusted God with this.

verses.zh: 他若专心为己，将灵和气收归自己，
verses.en: If God[NOTE:1] were to set his heart on it,[NOTE:2] and gather in his spirit[NOTE:3] and his breath,
notes: The preposition is implied from the first half of the verse.
Heb “he”; the referent (God) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

This is the reading following the Qere. The Kethib and the Syriac and the LXX suggest a reading יָשִׂים (yasim, “if he [God] recalls”). But this would require leaving out “his heart,” and would also require redividing the verse to make “his spirit” the object. It makes better parallelism, but may require too many changes.

verses.zh: 凡有血气的就必一同死亡；世人必仍归尘土。
verses.en: all flesh would perish together,and human beings would return to dust.

verses.zh: 你若明理，就当听我的话，留心听我言语的声音。
verses.en: “If you have[NOTE:1] understanding, listen to this,hear what I have to say.[NOTE:2]
notes: Or perhaps “Spirit,” though this may be less likely in close proximity with “breath.” As a reference to the human spirit cf. Ps. 104:29; as a reference to God’s Spirit originating with him, cf. Ps 104:30.
The phrase “you have” is not in the Hebrew text, but is implied.

verses.zh: 难道恨恶公平的可以掌权吗？那有公义的、有大能的，岂可定他有罪吗？
verses.en: Do you really think[NOTE:1] that one who hates justice can govern?[NOTE:2] And will you declare guilty the supremely Righteous One,[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “the sound of my words.”
The force of הַאַף (haʾaf) is “Is it truly the case?” The point is being made that if Job were right God could not be judging the world.

The verb חָבַשׁ (khavash) has the basic idea of “to bind,” as in binding on the yoke, and then in the sense of subduing people under authority (cf. Assyrian absanu). The imperfect verb here is best expressed with the potential nuance.

verses.zh: 他对君王说：你是鄙陋的；对贵臣说：你是邪恶的。
verses.en: who says to a king,[NOTE:1] ‘Worthless man,’[NOTE:2] and to nobles, ‘Wicked men,’
notes: The two words could be taken separately, but they seem to form a fine nominal hendiadys because the issue is God’s justice. So the word for power becomes the modifier.

Heb “Does one say,” although some smooth it out to say “Is it fit to say?” For the reading “who says,” the form has to be repointed to הַאֹמֵר (haʾomer) meaning, “who is the one saying.” This reading is supported by the LXX, Vulgate, and Syriac. Also it seems to flow better with the following verse. It would be saying that God is over the rulers and can rebuke them. The former view is saying that no one rebukes kings, much less Job rebuking God.

verses.zh: 他待王子不徇情面，也不看重富足的过于贫穷的，因为都是他手所造。
verses.en: who shows no partiality to princes,and does not take note of[NOTE:1] the rich more than the poorbecause all of them are the work of his hands?
notes: The word בְּלִיָּעַל (beliyyaʿal) means both “worthless” and “wicked.” It is common in proverbial literature, and in later writings it became a description of Satan. It is usually found with “son of.”

verses.zh: 在转眼之间，半夜之中，他们就死亡。百姓被震动而去世；有权力的被夺去非借人手。
verses.en: In a moment they die, in the middle of the night;[NOTE:1] people[NOTE:2] are shaken,[NOTE:3] and they pass away.The mighty are removed effortlessly.[NOTE:4]
notes: The verb means “to give recognition; to take note of” and in this passage with לִפְנֵי (lifne, “before”) it means to show preferential treatment to the rich before the poor. The word for “rich” here is an unusual word, found parallel to “noble” (Isa 32:2). P. Joüon thinks it is a term of social distinction (Bib 18 [1937]: 207-8).

Dhorme transposes “in the middle of the night” with “they pass away” to get a smoother reading. But the MT emphasizes the suddenness by putting both temporal ideas first. E. F. Sutcliffe leaves the order as it stands in the text, but adds a verb “they expire” after “in the middle of the night” (“Notes on Job, textual and exegetical,” Bib 30 [1949]: 79ff.).
R. Gordis (Job, 389) thinks “people” here mean the people who count, the upper class.

The verb means “to be violently agitated.” There is no problem with the word in this context, but commentators have made suggestions for improving the idea. The proposal that has the most to commend it, if one were inclined to choose a new word, is the change to יִגְוָעוּ (yigvaʿu, “they expire”; so Ball, Holscher, Fohrer, and others).

verses.zh: 神注目观看人的道路，看明人的脚步。
verses.en: For his eyes are on the ways of an individual;he observes all a person’s[NOTE:1] steps.
notes: Heb “not by hand.” This means without having to use force.

verses.zh: 没有黑暗、阴翳能给作孽的藏身。
verses.en: There is no darkness, and no deep darkness,where evildoers can hide themselves.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “his”; the referent (a person) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 神审判人，不必使人到他面前再三鉴察。
verses.en: For he does not still consider a person,[NOTE:1] that he should come before God in judgment.
notes: The construction of this colon uses the Niphal infinitive construct from סָתַר (satar, “to be hidden; to hide”). The resumptive adverb makes this a relative clause in its usage: “where the evildoers can hide themselves.”

verses.zh: 他用难测之法打破有能力的人，设立别人代替他们。
verses.en: He shatters the great without inquiry[NOTE:1] and sets up others in their place.
notes: Heb “for he does not put upon man yet.” This has been given a wide variety of interpretations, all of which involve a lot of additional thoughts. The word עוֹד (ʿod, “yet, still”) has been replaced with מוֹעֵד (moʿed, “an appointed time,” Reiske and Wright), with the ם (mem) having dropped out by haplography. This makes good sense. If the MT is retained, the best interpretation would be that God does not any more consider (from “place upon the heart”) man, that he might appear in judgment.

verses.zh: 他原知道他们的行为，使他们在夜间倾倒灭亡。
verses.en: Therefore, he knows their deeds;he overthrows them[NOTE:1] in the night,[NOTE:2] and they are crushed.
notes: Heb “[with] no investigation.”
The direct object “them” is implied and has been supplied in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 他在众人眼前击打他们，如同击打恶人一样。
verses.en: He strikes them for their wickedness[NOTE:1] in a place where people can see,[NOTE:2]
notes: The Hebrew term “night” is an accusative of time.

Heb “under wicked men,” or “under wickednesses.” J. C. Greenfield shows that the preposition can mean “among” as well (“Prepositions B Tachat in Jes 57:5, ” ZAW 32 [1961]: 227). That would allow “among wicked men.” It could also be “instead of” or even “in return for [their wickedness]” which is what the RSV does.

verses.zh: 因为他们偏行不跟从他，也不留心他的道，
verses.en: because they have turned away from following himand have not understood[NOTE:1] any of his ways,
notes: The text simply uses רֹאִים (roʾim): “[in the place where there are] seers,” i.e., spectators.

verses.zh: 甚至使贫穷人的哀声达到他那里；他也听了困苦人的哀声。
verses.en: so that they caused[NOTE:1] the cry of the poorto come before him,so that he hears[NOTE:2] the cry of the needy.
notes: The verb הִשְׂכִּילוּ (hiskilu) means “to be prudent; to be wise.” From this is derived the idea of “be wise in understanding God’s will,” and “be successful because of prudence”—i.e., successful with God.
The verse begins with the infinitive construct of בּוֹא (boʾ, “go”), showing the result of their impious actions.

verses.zh: 他使人安静，谁能扰乱（或译：定罪）呢？他掩面，谁能见他呢？无论待一国或一人都是如此―
verses.en: But if God[NOTE:1] is quiet, who can condemn[NOTE:2] him?If he hides his face, then who can see him?Yet[NOTE:3] he is over the individual and the nation alike,[NOTE:4]
notes: The verb here is an imperfect; the clause is circumstantial to the preceding clause, showing either the result, or the concomitant action.
Heb “he”; the referent (God) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

The verb in this position is somewhat difficult, although it does make good sense in the sentence—it is just not what the parallelism would suggest. So several emendations have been put forward, for which see the commentaries.

The line simply reads “and over a nation and over a man together.” But it must be the qualification for the points being made in the previous lines, namely, that even if God hides himself so no one can see, yet he is still watching over them all (see H. H. Rowley, Job [NCBC], 222).

verses.zh: 使不虔敬的人不得作王，免得有人牢笼百姓。
verses.en: so that the godless man should not ruleand not lay snares for the people.[NOTE:1]
notes: The word translated “alike” (Heb “together”) has bothered some interpreters. In the reading taken here it is acceptable. But others have emended it to gain a verb, such as “he visits” (Beer), “he watches over” (Duhm), “he is compassionate” (Kissane), etc. But it is sufficient to say “he is over.”

verses.zh: 有谁对　神说：我受了责罚，不再犯罪；
verses.en: “Has anyone said to God,‘I have endured chastisement,[NOTE:1] but I will not act wrongly any more;
notes: This last verse is difficult because it is unbalanced and cryptic. Some have joined the third line of v. 29 with this entire verse to make a couplet. But the same result is achieved by simply regarding this verse as the purpose of v. 29. But there still are some words that must be added. In the first colon, “[he is over the nations]…preventing from ruling.” And in the second colon, “laying” has to be supplied before “snares.”

verses.zh: 我所看不明的，求你指教我；我若作了孽，必不再作？
verses.en: teach me what I cannot see;[NOTE:1] if I have done evil, I will do so no more’?
notes: The Hebrew text has only “I lift up” or “I bear” (= I endure). The reading “I have been led astray” is obtained by changing the vowels to read a passive. If the MT is retained, an object has to be supplied, such as “chastisement” (so RSV, NASB) or “punishment” (NRSV). If not, then a different reading would be followed (e.g., “I was misguided” [NAB]; “I am guilty” [NIV]).

verses.zh: 他施行报应，岂要随你的心愿、叫你推辞不受吗？选定的是你，不是我。你所知道的只管说吧！
verses.en: Is it your opinion[NOTE:1] that God[NOTE:2] should recompense it,because you reject this?[NOTE:3] But you must choose, and not I,so tell us what you know.
notes: Heb “what I do not see,” more specifically, “apart from [that which] I see.”
Heb “is it from with you,” an idiomatic expression meaning “to suit you” or “according to your judgment.”
Heb “he”; the referent (God) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 明理的人和听我话的智慧人必对我说：
verses.en: Men of understanding say to me—any wise man listening to me says—

verses.zh: 约伯说话没有知识，言语中毫无智慧。
verses.en: that[NOTE:1] Job speaks without knowledgeand his words are without understanding.[NOTE:2]
notes: There is no object on the verb, and the meaning is perhaps lost. The best guess is that Elihu is saying Job has rejected his teaching.
Adding “that” in the translation clarifies Elihu’s indirect citation of the wise individuals’ words.

verses.zh: 愿约伯被试验到底，因他回答像恶人一样。
verses.en: But[NOTE:1] Job will be tested to the end,because his answers are like those of wicked men.
notes: The Hiphil infinitive construct is here functioning as a substantive. The word means “prudence; understanding.”

verses.zh: 他在罪上又加悖逆；在我们中间拍手，用许多言语轻慢　神。
verses.en: For he adds transgression[NOTE:1] to his sin;in our midst he claps his hands[NOTE:2] and multiplies his words against God.”
notes: The MT reads אָבִי (ʾavi, “my father”), which makes no sense. Some follow the KJV and emend the word to make a verb “I desire” or use the noun “my desire of it.” Others follow an Arabic word meaning “entreat, I pray” (cf. ESV, “Would that Job were tried”). The LXX and the Syriac versions have “but” and “surely” respectively. Since this is the only ms support, albeit weak, it may be the best choice. In this sense Elihu would be saying that because of Job’s attitude God will continue to test him.
Although frequently translated “rebellion,” the basic meaning of this Hebrew term is “transgression.”

"Bible
Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which
means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the
light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not
relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare
your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is
the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every
paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

- There are many textual issues in this chapter (especially Job 34:29-33). See UBS Text Project,
pp. 114-122 for details. The rare words, poetic imagery, and the shortening of phrases, which
a contemporary speaker would understand, are the things that cause confusion for modern
western thinkers/readers.

- Elihu, like the three comforters, calls on Job to hear, listen (IMPERATIVES,
cf. Job 32:10; 33:1,31,33; 34:2,10,16).

- Elihu defends the righteousness of God by disallowing the righteousness of Job.
"The two ways" must be true!

- Elihu presents his message by a series of rhetorical questions.

- Job 34:13 (twice), 17,18-19,33 expect a "no" answer

- Job 34:19 expects a "yes" answer

Remember, one major theme of Job is "who has true wisdom?"!

COHORTATIVES. They are related

34:5-6 "For Job has said. . ."
Elihu alludes to/quotes several statements of Job.

- "I am righteous" – Job 6:29; 9:20-21; 10:7; 12:4; 13:18; 27:5-6

- "God has taken away my rights" – Job 16:7-9,11-14; 27:2

- "My wound is incurable, though I am without transgression" – see #1 (cf. Job 6:4)

- "It profits a man nothing when he is pleased with God" – Job 21:14-15; 22:17

The interpretive question is who is the subject, Job (MT) or God (LXX,
TEV, NJB, REB)? Is Job the liar or is God? The issue is Job's defense of
being innocent. Is he innocent and God unfair? The UBS Text Project (p.
114) and the UBS Handbook (p. 620) suggest that the verse is
speaking of God's falsification of Job's legal case. Maybe God has
accepted the false accusations of the three comforters (cf. Job 13:4-10)
over Job's affirmation of innocence.

34:10-15 Elihu defends God's power and justice.

- He pays a man according to his work (cf. Job 4:8; 34:25; Ps. 28:4; 62:12; Pro. 12:14;
24:12; Eccl. 12:14; Jer. 17:10; 32:19; Ezek. 33:20; Matt. 16:27; 25:31-46; Rom. 2:6;
14:12; 1 Cor. 3:8; 2 Cor. 5:10; Gal. 6:7-10; 2 Tim. 4:14; 1 Pet. 1:17; Rev. 2:23; 20:12; 22:12)

- He is the sovereign creator, Job 34:13

- He is the sustainer of all life, Job 34:14-15

34:10 "men of understanding"
This is literally "men (BDB 35, KB 43) of heart" (BDB 523, KB 516).

▣ "far be it"
This idiomatic expression (like Paul's "God forbid," "may
it never be") is also found in Job 27:5.

34:12 This is the issue of the
book! Is God fair/just with His human creatures (cf. Job 8:3)? Elihu
says "yes"; Job says "no."

The book never really answers the question. It simply asserts God as
sovereign (i.e., Job 38:1-42:6)! The mystery remains but "the two
ways" does not fit all suffering and pain (i.e., Gen. 3:15; Psalm
22; Isaiah 53).

34:14 The question of this verse is "whose heart,
spirit, and breath" are being addressed:

- God's heart (JPSOA, Peshitta)

- humankind's spirit and breath (JPSOA, Peshitta)

The NKJV translates the three (i.e., heart, spirit, and breath) as
belonging to God.

Job 34:14-15 is contextually part of a hypothetical ("if")
sentence. In whatever way Job 34:14 is translated, Job 34:15 shows the
terrible result. Life would cease (cf. Job 12:10)!

34:15 "man would return to dust"
This is an allusion to Gen. 2:7 and 3:19. This imagery is used earlier
by Job in Job 10:9.

34:16-20 This strophe is directed
to Job (another hypothetical, BDB 49, Job 34:14,16). It mentions the
leaders who are rejected by God if they are not righteous (cf. Job 34:30).

- a king

- a judge (implied by use of "partiality")

- nobles (king's wealthy, powerful supporters)

- princes (king's family)

If they show partiality they will be removed. This may reflect Job's
claims/imagery in Job 29:25 or 31:37. Job may have been a regional
chief, surely a local elder.

34:17a "rule" This VERB (BDB 289, KB 289,
Qal IMPERFECT) normally means
"to bind," but it is used in several senses in Job.

- to bind up wounds, Job 5:18 (cf. Ps. 147:3)

- to dam up (i.e., bind) a stream, Job 28:11

- to govern/rule (i.e., bind up or control social life), Job 34:17

- to bind a covering on a dead body in the grave

In Gen. 22:3; 40:13; Num. 22:21; Jdgs. 19:10; 2 Sam. 16:1; 17:23; 19:26,
it means "to saddle" (several times in Kings). Only in this
context does it mean "to rule." NIDOTTE, vol. 2, p. 19,
suggests it may mean "to imprison," which seems to follow the
basic meaning of the Hebrew root better.

34:21-30 This strophe is parallel to Job 34:16-20. The God of justice
is characterized and the wicked are judged.

God is described as

- His eyes are upon the ways of human beings (cf. Job 34:11,25; 24:23b; 31:4)

- there is no darkness or deep shadow that can hide sinners from Him
(cf. Ps. 139:11-12; Jer. 23:24; Amos 9:2-3)

- His justice is fair and sure the first time (Job 34:23 may be an allusion to
Job's question in Job 24:1)

- He removes the wicked and establishes the righteous (notice the dashes after
Job 34:28 and before 34:30; RSV, NASB, NRSV use them to show that 34:30 relates
to 34:28)

The wicked described.

- they are judged publicly (this surely fits Job's life)

- because they have turned from His path

- because they have taken advantage of the poor

- they shall not rule (Job 34:30)

34:23 There is a textual question
with the ADVERB "yet"
(BDB 728). Many scholars emend it to "appointed time" (BDB
588, NRSV) but NASB and NKJV see "yet" used in the sense of
"further" (i.e., more time to examine). The UBS Text Project
(p. 116) gives "yet" an "A" rating (very high
probability).

34:28 God hears the cry of the
poor and afflicted but Elihu assumes Job has abused the poor and
powerless.

The question for Job is "Why has He not heard my cries?"

34:29 This verse addresses Job's complaint that God is hiding
from him, will not answer him. Sometime God does

- keep quiet (i.e., He is at rest and needs to be aroused)

- hide His face (cf. Job 13:24; Ps. 13:1; 44:24; 88:14; Isa. 45:15)

For both individuals (Job) and nations (i.e., I think the author is a
Judean sage), this verse hints at the corporate purpose of the book of
Job.

34:31-37 In this strophe Elihu
asserts Job's guilt by his previous words. Job has accused God of
injustice. If God is just, then Job must be unjust!

Notice the number of "I's" which Elihu attributes to Job's
false statements.

- I have borne chastisement, Job 34:31

- I will not offend anymore, Job 34:31

- I do not see (i.e., understand God), Job 34:32

- if I have done iniquity, I will do it no more, Job 34:32

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are
responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You,
the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this
section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

- Who are the wise men of Job 34:2,10,34?

- Why does Elihu quote/allude to Job's previous statements?

- Explain Job 34:9 in your own words.

- How does Job 34:11 characterize "the two ways"?

- Who is referred to in Job 34:17b?

- What does "God hides His face" mean (Job 34:29)?

- Does Job 34:31-32 describe Job's previous claims?

- To what does Job 34:37b refer?
